body_text: View All News Hilltop Holdings Inc. Announces Financial Results for Second Quarter 2026 July 23, 2026 Download (opens in new window) DALLAS--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Hilltop Holdings Inc. (NYSE: HTH) (“Hilltop”) today announced financial results for the second quarter of 2026. Hilltop produced income attributable to common stockholders of $36.5 million, or $0.63 per diluted share, for the second quarter of 2026, compared to $36.1 million, or $0.57 per diluted share, for the second quarter of 2025. Hilltop also announced that its Board of Directors declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.22 per common share, a 10% increase from the prior quarter, payable on August 21, 2026 to all common stockholders of record as of the close of business on August 7, 2026. Additionally, during the second quarter of 2026, Hilltop paid $47.0 million to repurchase an aggregate of 1,250,000 shares of its common stock at an average price of $37.58 per share pursuant to the 2026 stock repurchase program. These shares were returned to the pool of authorized but unissued shares of common stock. Furthermore, in July 2026, the Hilltop Board of Directors authorized an increase to the aggregate amount of common stock that Hilltop may repurchase under the aforementioned stock repurchase program to $200.0 million, an increase of $75.0 million. As a result of share repurchases during 2026, Hilltop has approximately $106 million of available share repurchase capacity through the expiration of the 2026 stock repurchase program in January 2027. The extent of the impact of uncertain economic conditions on our financial performance during the remainder of 2026 will depend in part on developments outside of our control, including, among others, changes in the political environment, the impact of tariffs and reciprocal tariffs, the timing and significance of further changes in U.S. Treasury yields and mortgage interest rates, and a volatile economic forecast. These conditions, coupled with exposure to changes in funding costs, inflationary pressures, elevated energy prices, and international armed conflicts and their impact on supply chains within our business segments during the second quarter of 2026 have had, and are expected to continue to have, an adverse impact on our operating results during the remainder of 2026. Jeremy B. Ford, Chairman, President and CEO of Hilltop, said, “During the second quarter of 2026, Hilltop delivered a 1% return on average assets and returned approximately $59 million to stockholders through dividends and share repurchases. At PlainsCapital Bank, continued core loan growth and an expansion in net interest margin drove a 1.3% return on average assets and $51 million of pre-tax income. PrimeLending realized a $2 million pre-tax loss on $2.4 billion of origination volume as the mortgage market faced a subdued start to the summer buying season primarily due to the recent increase in mortgage rates. HilltopSecurities produced a 10% pre-tax margin on $124 million of net revenues to deliver $12 million of pre-tax income, which was primarily driven by strong quarters in its Wealth Management and Structured Finance business lines. As we look to the second half of 2026, we expect to continue to execute on our strategic priorities while prudently managing capital and creating long-term value for our stockholders.” Second Quarter 2026 Highlights for Hilltop: The reversal of credit losses was $1.0 million during the second quarter of 2026, compared to a provision for credit losses of $1.8 million in the first quarter of 2026 and a reversal of credit losses of $7.3 million in the second quarter of 2025; The reversal of credit losses during the second quarter of 2026 was primarily driven by changes in the U.S. economic outlook associated with collectively evaluated loans and loan portfolio changes, partially offset by a build in the allowance related to specific reserves within the banking segment since the prior quarter. For the second quarter of 2026, net gains from sale of loans and other mortgage production income and mortgage loan origination fees was $78.9 million, compared to $80.7 million in the second quarter of 2025, a 2.2% decrease; Mortgage loan origination production volume was $2.4 billion during the second quarter of 2026, compared to $2.4 billion during the second quarter of 2025; Net gains from mortgage loans sold to third parties, including broker fee income, decreased to 229 basis points during the second quarter of 2026, compared to 261 basis points in the first quarter of 2026. Hilltop’s consolidated annualized return on average assets and return on average stockholders’ equity for the second quarter of 2026 were 0.99% and 6.89%, respectively, compared to 0.98% and 6.62%, respectively, for the second quarter of 2025; Hilltop’s book value per common share increased to $37.12 at June 30, 2026, compared to $36.63 at March 31, 2026; Hilltop’s total assets were $16.0 billion and $15.7 billion at June 30, 2026 and March 31, 2026, respectively; Loans 1, net of allowance for credit losses, were $8.2 billion and $8.0 billion at June 30, 2026 and March 31, 2026, respectively; Non-accrual loans were $54.8 million, or 0.57% of total loans, at June 30, 2026, compared to $61.0 million, or 0.66% of total loans, at March 31, 2026; Loans held for sale increased by 24.3% from March 31, 2026 to $1.0 billion at June 30, 2026; Total deposits 2 were $10.5 billion at each of June 30, 2026 and March 31, 2026; Hilltop maintained strong capital levels with a Tier 1 Leverage Ratio 3 of 12.73% and a Common Equity Tier 1 Capital Ratio of 18.34% at June 30, 2026; Hilltop’s consolidated net interest margin 4 increased to 3.21% for the second quarter of 2026, compared to 3.13% in the first quarter of 2026; For the second quarter of 2026, noninterest income was $200.0 million, compared to $192.6 million in the second quarter of 2025, a 3.8% increase; For the second quarter of 2026, noninterest expense was $266.7 million, compared to $261.2 million in the second quarter of 2025, a 2.1% increase; and Hilltop’s effective tax rate was 24.2% during the second quarter of 2026, compared to 23.4% during the same period in 2025. The conference call also will be webcast simultaneously on Hilltop’s Investor Relations website ( http://ir.hilltop.com ). About Hilltop Hilltop Holdings is a Dallas-based financial holding company. Its primary line of business is to provide business and consumer banking services from offices located throughout Texas through PlainsCapital Bank. PlainsCapital Bank’s wholly owned subsidiary, PrimeLending, provides residential mortgage lending throughout the United States. Hilltop Holdings’ broker-dealer subsidiaries, Hilltop Securities Inc. and Momentum Independent Network Inc., provide a full complement of securities brokerage, institutional and investment banking services in addition to clearing services and retail financial advisory. At June 30, 2026, Hilltop employed approximately 3,600 people and operated 304 locations in 47 states. Hilltop Holdings’ common stock is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and NYSE Texas under the symbol “HTH.” Find more information at Hilltop.com, PlainsCapital.com, PrimeLending.com and Hilltopsecurities.com. title: Understanding Structural Steel
summary: Structural steel may meet spec, but does it perform consistently? Learn how material variability impacts manufacturing and how to improve reliability.
body_text: Structural steel is often treated as a commodity—widely available, standardized, and seemingly interchangeable. Yet for manufacturers that depend on consistent performance in forming, welding, and fabrication, structural steel is rarely as simple as it appears. The challenge is not whether the material meets specification. The challenge is whether it performs consistently every time. As Kirk Erven, Technical Services Manager at Worthington Steel, explains, that distinction separates steel that merely meets requirements on paper from steel that delivers reliable results in production and in the field. This article will walk you through the following: What Is Structural Steel Why Structural Steel Is Used So Widely Where Strucutral Steel Challenges Actually Exist How Worthington Steel Suports Strucutral Steel Buyers A Simple Material That Requires the Right Approach What Is Structural Steel? At its core, structural steel refers to steel specifically designed for load-bearing applications. Unlike standard plain carbon steels that are primarily defined by chemistry, structural steels are largely driven by mechanical property requirements, including yield strength, ductility, toughness, and structural integrity under load. This category of steel is engineered to support heavy loads, absorb stress, resist impact, and maintain structural performance under demanding conditions. Common grades include 33, 40, 50, and 55, with the numbers representing minimum yield strength in KSI. While large-scale structures are the most visible examples, structural steel is also heavily used in component-driven applications. Worthington Steel regularly supports the production of floor decking, solar racking, agricultural equipment, and structural components for industrial applications where load-bearing performance and durability are critical. Why Structural Steel Is Used So Widely? Structural steel remains a core material across many industries because it offers a practical balance between performance, formability, weldability, toughness, and cost. Compared to HSLA steels, structural grades often provide a more economical solution while still delivering guaranteed mechanical properties. Compared to plain carbon steels, they provide more defined strength requirements and more predictable structural performance. Material Types General Characteristics Typical Tradeoff Plain Carbon Steel Primarily specified by chemistry with limited mechanical property requirements. Lowest cost, least performance control Structural Steel Mechanical property-driven steel with defined minimum strength requirements. Balance of cost, strength, and formability HSLA Steel Enhanced strength and consistency through tighter chemistry and processing control. Higher performance and consistency at a higher cost Impact resistance is also an important consideration in many structural applications, particularly where materials may experience repeated loading, environmental exposure, or dynamic stresses in the field. From a production standpoint, these grades are not considered highly difficult to manufacture. As Norm Bettedpur, Technical Services Manager, noted, "mills have got the practice down for structural grades," allowing them to be produced efficiently and at scale. That accessibility is one reason structural steel is often viewed as a commodity product. However, the tradeoff for that flexibility is that structural steel specifications often allow for a fairly wide range of acceptable mechanical properties. Two coils can technically meet the same grade requirement yet behave differently during downstream manufacturing. Customers often choose structural steel over HSLA because it offers an effective balance of strength, formability, and cost. However, that balance can come with a wider range of allowable mechanical properties. Achieving more predictable performance may require either a higher-cost material, such as HSLA, or stronger technical oversight throughout sourcing and processing to help minimize variation while maintaining the cost advantages of structural steel. That is where metallurgical expertise becomes critical. Where Structural Steel Challenges Actually Exist For many producers, the biggest challenge is not obtaining structural steel but ensuring the material performs consistently throughout manufacturing and in final application. Without reliable performance, issues such as excess scrap, forming instability, weld variability, lower production efficiency, and reduced product reliability can become more frequent. Even when steel meets the same grade specification, differences in chemistry, residual elements, rolling practices, and processing conditions can influence how the material behaves during forming, welding, and fabrication. As Erven and Bettedpur emphasized, customers often underestimate how much variation can exist within an acceptable specification range. Two coils may satisfy the same mechanical requirements yet behave differently enough to create production challenges. Those differences often become visible during downstream processing. Issues related to forming behavior, edge conditions, weld consistency, surface quality, or dimensional control can frequently be traced back to variations that are not immediately obvious on a certification sheet. Roll forming is one example where repeatability becomes especially important. Customers running continuous forming operations depend on material that behaves consistently, coil after coil. Small shifts in yield strength, elongation, or work hardening behavior can force repeated line adjustments, create dimensional variation, increase scrap, and reduce overall production efficiency. Paul Pfeifer, Technical Services Manager, described the role of the technical team as helping to "ensure steel performs consistently to customer satisfaction." That responsibility goes far beyond simply sourcing steel to a specification." That responsibility goes far beyond simply sourcing steel to a specification. It involves understanding the customer's application, manufacturing process, and performance expectations to ensure the material behaves as intended in real production environments. Erven reinforced that this alignment is especially important early in the design process. If material behavior is not properly considered up front, downstream corrections can become significantly more expensive and difficult to implement later. In structural steel applications, performance depends on the entire system working together, including sourcing strategy, material properties, processing controls, forming behavior, and final application requirements. When any one of those elements falls out of alignment, performance issues can follow. How Worthington Steel Supports Structural Steel Buyers In a market where structural steel is often viewed as a commodity, Worthington Steel takes a more integrated, application-focused approach. The goal is not simply to supply material, but to help ensure it performs reliably within each customer's manufacturing environment. That process begins with technical expertise. Worthington Steel's Technical Services team combines deep experience in metallurgy, mill-side steel production, downstream processing, and end-use application performance to help bridge the gap between steel specifications and real-world manufacturing demands. As Bettedpur explained, the team works to "bridge the gap between mills and customers," combining knowledge of how steel is produced with how it ultimately performs in the application. Beyond technical support, production consistency plays a critical role in the performance of structural steel. Chemistry is only part of the equation. Maintaining controlled rolling conditions, annealing parameters, and processing standards throughout production is equally important to achieving reliable results. As Erven noted, "We are making a specific product for a specific order for a specific customer." He further explained that production is guided by defined processing "recipes" tailored to the final application: "We know what we need to do to produce those final properties." By working closely with both mills and customers, Worthington Steel helps identify and manage variability before it becomes a downstream manufacturing issue. Supply chain flexibility is another important advantage. As Bettedpur noted, "having access to multiple sources through a single entity like Worthington Steel with strong mill partners can make a huge difference." That access helps customers maintain continuity of supply while supporting dependable performance expectations across sourcing options. In addition, Worthington Steel's value-added processing capabilities allow teams to further tailor material to specific application requirements, including tighter tolerances, coating solutions, surface characteristics, and forming performance. Testing, analysis, and metallurgical support help validate performance expectations before material reaches the customer's production line, reducing risk and supporting long-term reliability in the field. The result is steel engineered not only to meet specifications, but to deliver predictable performance in demanding real-world applications. For customers, that means greater confidence that the material will perform as expected, from initial processing through final use in the field. A Simple Material That Requires the Right Approach Structural steel may not carry the same level of technical complexity as high carbon or specialty alloys, but its performance is no less critical. What appears to be a straightforward material is heavily dependent on repeatable performance, application alignment, and processing control. For customers, success comes from understanding that structural steel is not purely a commodity purchase. Achieving reliability requires the right material selection, the right processing controls, and the right technical support. Just as importantly, involving a knowledgeable processor early in the design and sourcing process can help prevent downstream production challenges, costly rework, and time-consuming root cause investigations later on. In structural applications, meeting the specification is only part of the equation. Long-term success depends on selecting material that not only meets requirements on paper but also performs reliably throughout manufacturing and in the field. We provide advanced material support , price risk management , supply chain solutions , and the highest level of customer service and collaboration. Employer of Record (EOR) software is a category of HR tech that lets companies hire workers in foreign countries without setting up a local legal entity. The EOR becomes the legal employer on paper, handling payroll, taxes, benefits, and local labor law compliance on behalf of the hiring company. You retain day-to-day control over the work your team members do. In practice, EOR software sits at the intersection of legal infrastructure and HR operations. It gives you a dashboard to onboard new hires, run payroll across currencies, and manage contracts, all without piecing together data from separate tools at month-end. Who typically uses EOR software? EOR software tends to fit a few specific situations well: Startups and scale-ups hiring their first international team members, where the cost and time of entity setup in a new country would far outweigh the headcount being brought on. Teams comparing EOR software for tech startups often find this the fastest path to compliant hiring. Companies testing a new market before committing to a permanent local presence. HR and finance teams managing distributed workforces across multiple countries who want one place to track payroll, contracts, and compliance instead of working across multiple local vendors. Here's what the evaluation looked at: Country coverage and entity model: how many countries are supported, and whether the provider uses owned legal entities or relies on third-party partner networks. Onboarding speed: how quickly a new hire moves from offer to active employment. Pricing transparency: whether fees are published upfront and reflect the full cost of employment, beyond the base EOR fee. Compliance depth: tax automation, how frequently local law updates are applied, and whether IP protection is built into every employment contract. Integration ecosystem: connectivity with common HR, payroll, and finance tools. Product scope: whether the provider goes beyond pure EOR into recruiting, US payroll, contractor management, or AI-powered workflows. Company size fit: suitability for early-stage startups, growing teams, and enterprises. Payroll accuracy of 99.8%, with runs that are up to 80% faster than managing payroll manually or across disconnected systems. FAQ How do I choose the right EOR software from options like Bolto, Remote, Multiplier, Oyster HR, and G-P? Start by matching your stage and hiring volume to the product. Early-stage teams making their first one or two international hires tend to do well with guided, self-serve options like Oyster HR, while companies scaling across many countries simultaneously need deeper compliance infrastructure and faster onboarding timelines, which is where Bolto and G-P tend to fit better. Budget, support model, and whether you need recruiting built in are the three factors that narrow the list fastest. Is Bolto better than Remote or Oyster HR for startups hiring their first international employee? For startups that need speed and want recruiting, payroll, and compliance in one place, Bolto's 48-hour onboarding and AI-powered candidate shortlisting within 72 hours give it an edge over Remote and Oyster HR, both of which focus on EOR and payroll without integrated talent sourcing. When should I consider G-P instead of Bolto or Multiplier for international hiring? G-P fits best when you are running high-volume, multi-country hiring programs at an enterprise scale and your legal or finance team needs deep in-country compliance infrastructure across 180+ countries. For early-stage or growth-stage companies that want faster setup, more pricing flexibility, and recruiting built into the same workflow, Bolto or Multiplier are likely a better fit for your current stage. What is the difference between EOR software and a PEO, and which do I need? An EOR becomes the legal employer in a country where you have no local entity, making it the right choice for international hires. A Professional Employer Organization (PEO) operates as a co-employer, which requires you to already have a legal entity in the country where you are hiring. If you are hiring internationally without a local entity, you need EOR software; if you are managing US payroll and HR under your own entity, a PEO may be the better fit. How do I weigh whether Remofirst's lower pricing is worth the trade-offs compared to Bolto or Multiplier? Remofirst's lower per-head cost works well if your priority is keeping early international hiring costs down and you can accept a leaner feature set with less integration depth. As your team scales, gaps in onboarding speed, compliance automation, and integrations with your HR and finance stack tend to become more expensive to work around than the per-seat savings support, which is where platforms like Bolto or Multiplier recoup their higher starting cost. title: Entergy Arkansas helps power possibility at Hope Landing
summary: Every year, Entergy Arkansas invests in the communities it serves because powering life means more than delivering electricity, it means creating opportunities for people to thrive.
body_text: Every year, Entergy Arkansas invests in the communities it serves because powering life means more than delivering electricity, it means creating opportunities for people to thrive. As part of that commitment, the company awarded more than $2.1 million in grants to more than 420 nonprofit partners and community organizations in 2025, supporting programs that strengthen communities, improve quality of life and help power the next generation of Arkansas. One of those organizations is Hope Landing in El Dorado. Their mission: every child deserves the opportunity to reach their fullest potential. At Hope Landing, approximately 700 children receive more than 30,000 physical, occupational, speech, equine and aquatic therapy sessions each year. Every visit is another opportunity to grow stronger, become more confident and achieve what once seemed impossible. “It’s so rewarding to see these kids inside and out here get on a horse and overcome their fears, their insecurities, their sensory deficits and hearing their first words on a horse,” said Kaitlin Coston, Hope Landing equine therapist. Since 2019, Entergy Arkansas has supported Hope Landing’s equestrian therapy program, helping ensure children from across south Arkansas and neighboring states have access to specialized therapies that can change lives. For Entergy Arkansas Customer Service Region Manager Chris Wasson, that mission became deeply personal. After his son, Rhett, was diagnosed with special needs, his family turned to Hope Landing for therapy, never imagining that the organization his company had supported for years would one day become part of their own story. “We’ve seen him take leaps and bounds in terms of his ability to do different things,” Chris said. One milestone, in particular, still stands out. “When he first came to Hope Landing, he couldn’t step over a threshold that was a couple of inches high,” Chris said. As therapy continued, that small obstacle became another victory. “At our house we have a little playground with a border around it and it’s about four to six inches high and it wasn’t long later he was able to step over that by himself. While it seems small to us, it was big for him,” Chris said. Hope Landing’s impact reaches far beyond physical milestones. “They teach him to overcome obstacles both figuratively and literally. It’s been tremendous to see his growth here,” Chris said. With each step, word and challenge conquered, Chris said it’s meaningful to see the missions of Hope Landing and Entergy Arkansas come together. “Hope Landing’s vision is to give hope and a purpose to children with different abilities and help them reach their God-given potential. Entergy’s vision is we power life. My family has seen both of those visions interconnect,” he said. By investing in organizations like Hope Landing, Entergy Arkansas is helping children build the confidence, independence and opportunities they need to thrive—creating stronger communities today while helping power the next generation of Arkansas for years to come.
